questions.q: In the Meridian Supply Co. case study, what did the Chapter 1 profiling step measure for each source CRM, and what did it find?
options: Nothing was measured — the team relied entirely on impressions of data quality
Only record counts, with no measure of duplication at all
Uniqueness, using a Matching Rule/Duplicate Rule pass on sample extracts, finding Meridian at 92% unique and Source B at 78% unique
File storage volume for ContentVersion records
questions.explain: Profiling ran a real, measured Matching Rule/Duplicate Rule pass (set to Report) against sample extracts, producing specific uniqueness figures for each source rather than relying on guesswork.

questions.q: What migration strategy did Meridian's leadership sign off on, and why?
options: A phased migration — Meridian's own data first, then Source B's once its de-duplication logic was designed and tested
Big bang, migrating both companies' data in one event to minimize project duration
No formal strategy was chosen; data was loaded as convenient
A strategy that migrated only Opportunities, excluding Accounts and Contacts entirely
questions.explain: Leadership chose a phased strategy: Meridian's lower-risk data first, Source B's data second, specifically after the de-duplication challenges specific to Source B could be properly designed and tested.

questions.q: What specific complication did Chapter 3 validation reveal that the original Chapter 1 profiling hadn't been designed to catch?
options: A sequencing error loading Opportunities before Accounts
Nearly 3,000 cross-source duplicates — Source B Contacts that likely represented the same real people as existing Meridian Contacts
A file-size limit being exceeded during the Bulk API 2.0 load
A missing rollback trigger definition
questions.explain: The original profiling measured duplicates within each source independently. The cross-source duplicate problem — the same real person represented in both companies' data — only became visible once the two sources were compared together during rehearsal validation.

questions.q: Why was re-running the corrected Source B load, after building the cross-source de-duplication pass, described as "safe and fast"?
options: Because the legacy Source B system had already been decommissioned
Because Hard Delete was used to remove all previously loaded records first
Because the Data Import Wizard was used instead of Data Loader for the re-run
Because the team had used upsert against a real External ID from the first rehearsal attempt, making the load idempotent and safely re-runnable
questions.explain: Because External IDs and upsert were used from the very first rehearsal attempt, re-running the load after fixing the de-duplication logic simply re-confirmed correct records and corrected the rest, without creating duplicates.

questions.q: What was the single most common hypercare ticket during Source B's post-migration support window, and why was it resolved quickly?
options: A rollback request, resolved by restoring the pre-cutover backup
A request to extend the freeze window, resolved by delaying cutover
A sales rep looking for a Contact that had been merged rather than lost, resolved quickly because the merge was fully documented
A request to re-enable disabled validation rules that had been forgotten
questions.explain: Because the cross-source merge decision was fully documented (per Lesson 17's triage approach), hypercare staff could quickly explain to reps that a 'missing' Contact had actually been merged into an existing record, not lost.
